analysis.one_liner: Lets student loan borrowers refinance older loans at lower fixed rates, paid for by a 30% minimum tax on million-dollar incomes.
analysis.headline: On June 11, 2014, 56 senators voted to take up the bill, but that fell short of the 60 needed, so it never came to an up-or-down vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let borrowers refinance federal, older bank-issued, and private student loans made before July 2013 into federal loans at the lower fixed interest rates in effect for the 2013-14 school year. Eligibility would be weighted toward borrowers with the greatest financial need, and private lenders would have to report data on their loan books to regulators. The cost would be covered by a new minimum tax: anyone with adjusted gross income over $1 million would pay at least 30% of income above a charitable-deduction threshold.
analysis.who_benefits: Student loan borrowers with loans taken out before July 1, 2013 — including federal Direct Loans, older bank-issued FFEL loans, and private student loans — who would see their interest rates dropped to the fixed 2013-14 rates for the life of the loan, lowering their monthly payments and total interest. Eligibility rules would be designed to favor borrowers in the greatest financial need, and borrowers would keep credit toward income-driven repayment and public-service forgiveness built up on their original loans.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Education Department to refinance unpaid principal, accrued interest, and late charges on federal Direct Loans and older FFEL loans first disbursed before July 1, 2013, at the fixed interest rates in effect for the 12 months beginning July 1, 2013.

Creates a program to refinance private student loans into federal Direct loans at the same fixed rates, limited to borrowers in good standing and with eligibility rules aimed at those in greatest financial need, and requiring loan counseling first.
Preserves borrowers' progress toward income-based repayment and the public-service repayment plan by counting payments made on the original loan.

Pays for the program with a 'fair share tax' requiring taxpayers with adjusted gross income over $1 million to pay a minimum 30% rate on income above a modified charitable deduction, and requires any leftover revenue to go to deficit reduction.

Requires the Education Department and the consumer bureau to run a public campaign alerting borrowers that they may be eligible, and requires private lenders to report loan data to regulators and Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Households with income over $1 million, who would face the new 30% minimum tax, and private student lenders, whose high-interest loans would be paid off and replaced with cheaper federal loans. The federal government would also take on the refinanced loan balances; the bill requires the refinancing programs to shut down once their net cost equals the new tax revenue or after two years, whichever comes first.

drawbacks.text: The federal government would absorb the full cost of the refinanced loans while critics argued the millionaires' tax revenue was not a real offset, so taxpayers could end up on the hook if refinanced borrowers' repayments or defaults came in worse than projected.
Refinanced private loans would be excluded from loan forgiveness and public-service repayment programs, so borrowers who converted private loans would permanently give up those benefits.
The program is a one-time fix for existing loans; it does nothing to lower the cost of college for future students, and it sunsets within two years.
The program is limited to loans disbursed before July 1, 2013, and requires borrowers to be in good standing, so borrowers already in default would not qualify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers locked into rates from before mid-2013, the bill offered a real, direct cut in interest costs, and the tax fell entirely on incomes above $1 million. The honest objections are that the federal government takes on all the refinanced debt while its revenue estimate is built on a tax whose collections are uncertain, that defaulted borrowers — often the worst off — are excluded, and that it leaves the underlying price of college untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate voted 56-38 on June 11, 2014 to start debating the bill, but that procedural vote needed 60, so the bill never got an up-or-down vote; later motions to try again went nowhere.

narrative.text: Warren introduced the bill on June 4, 2014 with 44 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents.
The Senate held a cloture vote on the motion to proceed on June 11, 2014; it failed 56-38, short of the 60 votes needed to begin debate.
The Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee held a hearing on the bill on July 31, 2014, but the bill was never reported out or brought back to the floor for a vote.
Senators made four further motions to proceed in September 2014, none of which led to a vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $1 million kept paying taxes at the existing rates instead of the 30% minimum, and private student lenders kept their pre-2013 loan books earning higher interest. Borrowers with older loans continue paying their original higher rates.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell

sides.party_line_note: The June 11 vote split almost entirely by party: 51 of 53 Democrats and both independents voted yes, while only 3 of 45 Republicans did, leaving the bill 4 votes short of the 60 needed.

industries.note: Borrowers could have paid off high-interest private loans with cheaper fixed-rate federal loans, and the bill ordered regulators to design eligibility rules that 'preclude windfall profits' for lenders. It also required private lenders to report default and delinquency data on their loan books to Congress and regulators.
Older bank-issued FFEL loans would be paid off in full and converted into federal Direct loans, ending the lenders' ongoing interest and servicing income on those loans.
A new 30% minimum tax on income above a charitable-deduction allowance would have raised these taxpayers' bills to fund the refinancing program.
